pages.title: The clearing remembers — Arrival
pages.narrative_job: The stream kept its own time. Wilson had been at the clearing since the first light reached the old stones, his axe rising and falling over ground worn by years of practice. Jake had come for quiet, not company. He stopped when four hooves turned toward him. The water went on moving. Neither mentioned the lake or the carnival until Wilson broke the silence. “You picked a fine morning to interrupt.” Jake glanced at the space between the boulders. “I was looking for somewhere nobody wanted anything.” Wilson raised his axe. “Then you took the wrong path.”

pages.title: The bank knows its own — Arrival
pages.narrative_job: Mist covered the water, but it could not hide the old boards of the hunting cabin. One newer plank lay among the dark timber of the dock; the half-sunken boat still pulled gently at its tether. Bobby waited on the raised bank. Phillip approached with three heads watching the cabin, water and ground in turn, all carried by one body. “After last week, you must be feeling dangerous.” Bobby gave him a long look. “You came all this way to ask?” The water moved beneath the dock. Phillip had expected a short visit; the swamp had offered no such promise.

pages.title: A toast in the hills — Arrival
pages.narrative_job: The cabin windows were warm against the cold hillside. Zach shook the wind from his shoulders and accepted the invitation without a purchase agreement. Kevin had set two glasses on the old table. “To the chairman,” he said. “And to David, wherever he's found a chair.” Zach laughed. “Preferably one with a view.” They toasted victories and the peculiar trouble of winning an argument with Babb. A gust struck the shutters. Kevin looked toward the room's far side, then back at his guest. Zach noticed the pause, but not its meaning. The evening had begun courteously enough.

pages.title: What the road remembers — Arrival
pages.narrative_job: The early light had scarcely reached the trees when rain began to darken the track. Ben knew what a familiar road could become in weather. Last week's wrong turn had taught him that recognition was not the same as certainty. From the truck he watched the verge disappear into mist, then glanced back toward the road he could still recognize. A gust shook leaves from the branches. He had started the morning convinced that he had somewhere to be. Now the weather was asking whether the road would let him get there.
